title: From wastes to therapeutic treasure: phytochemistry, molecular docking, and DFT-based reactivity profiling of walnut green husk and shell
content: Agricultural by-products have attracted increasing scientific interest because of their rich phytochemical profiles and potential for use in various applications. The present study investigated the phytochemical composition, antioxidant activity, enzyme-inhibitory properties, and cytotoxic effects of the green husk and shell of Juglans regia L. (Juglandaceae). Ethyl acetate (EA), acetone, 70% acetone (hydroacetone), and aqueous extracts were obtained by maceration. Among the extracts examined, the hydroacetone extract of the shell contained the highest total phenolic content (67.43 mg gallic acid equivalent (GAE) per g), whereas the acetone extract of the green husk showed the greatest total flavonoid content (21.33 mg rutin equivalent (RE) per g). HPLC/MS profiling identified a diverse array of bioactive constituents like caffeic acid, protocatechuic acid, p-coumaric acid derivative, juglanins B and C, and hydrojuglone glucoside, and their distribution varied according to both the walnut fruit part and the extraction solvent. The hydroacetone shell extract exhibited the strongest antioxidant performance in the radical-scavenging activities, as well as reducing capacities. The aqueous shell extract and hydroacetone green husk extract showed the highest metal chelating activity, with values of 16.20 and 16.02 mg EDTAE per g, respectively. Similarly, the hydroacetone and aqueous shell extracts showed the greatest total antioxidant capacity (2.46 and 2.34 mmol trolox equivalent (TE) per g, respectively). Regarding enzyme inhibition, the hydroacetone and acetone extracts of the green husk recorded the highest acetylcholinesterase (2.77 mg galantamine equivalent (GALAE) per g) and butyrylcholinesterase (3.39 mg GALAE per g) inhibitory activity. The EtOAc shell extract revealed the highest tyrosinase (65.80 mg kojic acid equivalent (KAE) per g) and α-glucosidase (7.37 mmol acarbose equivalent (ACAE) per g) inhibitory activities, as well as cytotoxicity against the colorectal carcinoma (HCT-116) cell line (IC50 93.50 µg mL−1). To complement the experimental findings, network pharmacology, machine-learning analysis, and molecular docking were employed to explore compound–target associations and provide a computational assessment of the potential interactions of selected phytochemicals with relevant biological targets. These findings support the potential valorisation of these underutilized walnut by-products as natural sources of biologically active compounds for future food, pharmaceutical, and other biotechnological applications.
